title: ICRIR on the Troubles Bill: information sharing, resources and family confidence
label: 11 November 2026 · ICRIR follow-up
summary: The Independent Commission for Reconciliation and Information Recovery (ICRIR) told MPs that co-operation from the Republic of Ireland on sharing sensitive material remains stalled, that the organisation is under-resourced for the likely workload and has submitted a major business case for added funding, and that recent legal and procedural changes in the Troubles Bill create opportunities and tensions—especially over national security redactions and the Attorney General’s consent to prosecutions. The witnesses defended the value of ICRIR’s investigative approach for families, described progress on implementing a critical internal review, and warned that a failure to fund the work would push relatives towards expensive public inquiries.

glossary.definition: Independent Commission for Reconciliation and Information Recovery, the body conducting legacy investigations in Northern Ireland.
The successor body envisaged once the Troubles Bill is passed in both the UK and Ireland.
An Garda Síochána, the police service of the Republic of Ireland.
International Letter of Request—formal legal requests between states for evidence or witness cooperation.
The Northern Ireland prosecuting authority that issues formal requests like ILRs and decides on prosecutions.
The UK Government minister with powers under the Bill to review and withhold sensitive material on national security grounds.
Hearings led by an investigating body to establish facts, rather than adversarial courtroom trials.
Annually Managed Expenditure, a Treasury budgeting category used here for the commission’s unusual funding profile.

chapters.title: Irish co-operation remains stalled
chapters.takeaway: ICRIR has asked the Garda for material covering border deaths but has received only acknowledgements; a political, cross-border solution is needed to share sensitive information.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Sir Declan, you wrote about information sharing with Ireland—have arrangements improved since June?

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: No. We've sent about 12 letters asking for help on border cases and had only acknowledgements, no substantive disclosure.

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: The difficulty is legal and political: the UK protects national security material tightly and Ireland has similar concerns, so you need a political agreement between governments.

turns.speaker: Adam Jogee
turns.text: Kenova worked with An Garda Síochána—why can’t the ICRIR get similar co-operation?

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: Kenova was a PSNI criminal investigation. ICRIR is not a law enforcement body, so it cannot issue ILRs; only the Public Prosecution Service can do that for criminal probes.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You said 11 requests to the Garda covered 31 deaths—did any produce material?

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: No substantive material so far. The Garda told us politically they aren't in a position to provide it before both jurisdictions have passed matching legislation.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How many cases are affected by that lack of co-operation?

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: About 500 deaths along the border involve people and groups who say they won't engage unless Irish material can be secured—Warrenpoint, for example, was detonated from the Republic.

chapters.title: Legal design of the Bill raises practical and political questions
chapters.takeaway: The Bill creates new powers and oversight, but features like Attorney General consent and national security redactions could be contentious and need careful handling.

turns.speaker: Mr Kohler
turns.text: The Bill requires Attorney General consent to serious prosecutions—what do you make of that?

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: Legally it should produce the same result as the PPS, but some will see it as political. Judicial review is always possible, so this is partly a political judgment.

turns.speaker: Mr Kohler
turns.text: Would that clause threaten co-operation with Ireland?

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: It could be one of several sticking points. I hope both governments will be 'grown up' and trade concessions where needed to aid victims and families.

turns.speaker: Sir Alec Shelbrooke
turns.text: The Bill wants to avoid needless duplication of past investigations—how will you decide when to re-interview people?

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: If there's already a detailed statement from an earlier inquiry, it should be the starting point. You'd only re-interview if there is new material or a central player wasn't previously questioned.

turns.speaker: Sir Alec Shelbrooke
turns.text: The Secretary of State can block disclosure for national security—any safeguards you'd like?

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: We welcome the commission's power to appeal the Secretary of State's national security decisions; being able to challenge those determinations should boost public confidence.

turns.speaker: Simon Hoare
turns.text: Some fear 'national security' gets used to hide embarrassing facts—do you think the appeal power will curb that?

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: Yes. We will see the material and can take a view; if we suspect misuse we'd be able to take it to a tribunal, which should discourage improper blanket claims.

chapters.title: Workload, staffing and funding are urgent problems
chapters.takeaway: ICRIR is operating with far fewer investigators than it needs, has a large pipeline of cases, and has submitted a major business case for more money; failure to fund risks many expensive public inquiries.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Amanda, you asked for amendments so originators don't have to tag sensitivity—what burden would that remove?

turns.speaker: Amanda Logan
turns.text: Currently agencies mark material 'Legacy Act sensitive' when they send it; if the commission had to decide all tags we'd face extra workload and would need close partnership with originators anyway.

turns.speaker: Amanda Logan
turns.text: We need many more investigators. An independent panel advised around nine syndicates (about 58 investigators each) reduced to seven with AI—over 400 staff. We currently have 189 operational staff.

turns.speaker: Ronnie Armour
turns.text: We submitted a business case in summer seeking £628 million total—this includes the existing £232 million and the costs of inquisitorial proceedings and scaling up staff.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How much has the commission spent so far and is it value for money?

turns.speaker: Ronnie Armour
turns.text: By end of 2025-26 we drew down just over £77m and actual spend is about £64–65m, so there’s an underspend largely explained by accounting matters; value judgment depends on delivering outcomes.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What if the business case is refused—do you have contingency plans?

turns.speaker: Ronnie Armour
turns.text: We are planning for the next year with the funds we know about—roughly £150–160m left—but not getting the extra funding would significantly reduce our capacity to deliver.

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: We currently have around 159 investigations in eligibility and another 57 waiting—over 200 investigations covering 293 deaths and 310 requestors, with some very resource-heavy cases like Guildford and Warrenpoint.

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: If we cannot resource this properly, families will push for public inquiries, which are far costlier and slower—so underfunding risks a big political and fiscal problem later.

turns.speaker: Mr Kohler
turns.text: Do you have an estimate of total investigations you expect?

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: Our central estimate is about 650 investigations over the workplan, aiming for nearly 80–90 outcomes per year once scaled up; we target a flow of cases to produce a steady output.

chapters.title: Implementing Peter May recommendations and internal culture
chapters.takeaway: Most of the 19 recommendations from the Peter May review are done; three remain active and the commission has strengthened governance, finance and staff engagement but cultural work continues.

turns.speaker: Mr Kohler
turns.text: Where are you on implementing the 19 Peter May recommendations?

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: I met Peter May regularly while we implemented the report; we’ve moved into business-as-usual sponsorship on remaining items.

turns.speaker: Ronnie Armour
turns.text: Only three recommendations remain active. We've set up a finance committee with an independent chair, strengthened governance and sponsorship with the NIO, and improved staff relations.

turns.speaker: Ronnie Armour
turns.text: The remaining work includes clarifying line management roles, a formal lessons-learned programme to run once more cases reach reporting stage, and deeper AME budgeting understanding.

turns.speaker: Mr Kohler
turns.text: How are you assessing cultural change inside the commission?

turns.speaker: Ronnie Armour
turns.text: We've run a staff pulse survey showing commitment but concerns about internal communication and leadership cohesion; we've engaged an organisational consultant and formal industrial relations with PCS.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Do you still meet Peter May?

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: Regular meetings have stopped; we now meet him at public events. He was an external contractor rather than a standing member of the commission.

chapters.title: Reports and family engagement shape public confidence
chapters.takeaway: The commission emphasises personal engagement with families, sometimes sharing more detail privately than in published reports, and believes early positive reports build trust, but publication timing and sensitivities are tricky.

turns.speaker: Chris Bloore
turns.text: The first report in September moved families—how will you persuade other families and campaigns, like Birmingham, to trust ICRIR rather than demand public inquiries?

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: You must recognise families often feel mistreated by past processes. As we publish credible outcomes and engage personally with families, confidence will grow; having more linked cases can also help.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Do families get more detail in private than appears in the public report?

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: Yes. We discuss findings with requestors throughout the investigation and sometimes share details not in the published report, while protecting genuinely sensitive material and avoiding risk to families.

turns.speaker: Chris Bloore
turns.text: Some critics say reports just re-review existing material without new lines of investigation—do you accept that?

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: In some cases we won't find new material and we must be honest about that; but it still matters that families can see every stone has been turned and that an independent, rigorous process was applied.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Publication delays: you had two cases spending two months at the Secretary of State’s office for security checking—can that be faster?

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: Ideally, agencies would respond quicker so the Secretary of State need not use the full 60-day period. We hope the process will be streamlined, but national security checks can be slow.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: One final point: some families fear publication because they live locally—how do you address that?

turns.speaker: Sir Declan Morgan
turns.text: We must be family-centred: tailor reports, protect identities where necessary, and avoid placing families at risk while still giving truthful outcomes. That balance is central to our approach.
